title: Burgundy’s Crémant starts its earliest harvest
summary:
Burgundy is seeing one of the earliest harvests for Crémant this year, with some producers having already started picking over the weekend.

The post Burgundy’s Crémant starts its earliest harvest appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: Burgundy is seeing one of the earliest harvests for Crémant this year, with some producers having already started picking over the weekend. Winemaker Marc Sangoy, president of the Cave de Lugny, told AFP that the producer had started picking on 8 August, an advance on the previous early harvest record, which was set in 2022, on 13 August. Sangoy, who is president of the cooperative in Saône-et-Loire which has around 1,250 hectares of vines, said that he had never experienced harvests this early in his forty-year career. He said the optimum moment for the Crémant de Bourgogne, which must not exceed 11.5° ABV, had come early. “If you know how to harvest it at the right time, quickly enough, yes, it will be a good, well-balanced vintage." One picker in Burgundy was quoted by local news site france3-regions as saying they were “very surprised” at the grapes, which he had expected to be dry due to the droughts, but which were in fact “beautiful bunches". One advantage of the drought is the lack of mildew, associated with wet conditions, so the grapes are very healthy.  However yields have been affected, particularly in the case of younger plants that are less able to resist the heat as effectively, and flowers getting burned by the sun has also resulted in smaller grapes, with less juice. Meanwhile the red and white wine harvest is expected to start later than anticipated. According to Burgundy Winegrowers’ Association the CAVB (the Confédération des appellations et des vignerons de Bourgogne), an early harvest date of around 15 August had been initially expected, however the heat waves and droughts not only stunted the growth of the vines, but also slowed the ripening process. It is now expected to start around ten days later, on 25 August. However, early prognosis suggests that the yield could be half that of a normal year.

title: All eyes on the mid-strength beer trend
summary:
Australia’s Cascade Brewery has jumped on the trend for mid-strength beer with the introduction of its first mid-strength brew to have been produced in the beer company’s history. db looks at the trend.

The post All eyes on the mid-strength beer trend appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Australia’s Cascade Brewery has jumped on the trend for mid-strength beer with the introduction of its first mid-strength brew to have been produced in the beer company’s history. db looks at the trend. The new 3.5% ABV beer, named Cascade Draught, marks the only mid-strength beer variation the brewery has ever created and has been designed to match the brewery’s original full-strength line-up.

A global trend

This is not the first time mid-strength beer trends have swept the globe this year with a raft of breweries across the US also rebuilding their adoration for the style in a bid to help distinguish such beers from light and non-alcoholic brews as well as full-strength offerings. The beer from Cascade Brewery, which has been formulated as a slightly lower-alcohol alternative to an already-popular brew which “has been part of Tasmania for more than six decades, so when we created a mid-strength version, we knew we had to get it right,” said Cascade Brewery head of manufacturing Brendan Flanagan. Flanagan explained to Inside FMCG: “This is a good example of how we’re investing to ensure Cascade continues to brew beer in Tasmania for Tasmanians for years to come.”

An investment for the future

The product launch also follows the company’s recent investments into restoring the infrastructure of its production facility. The mid-strength beer will be available in 30-packs of 375ml cans, the product is distributed exclusively within the Tasmanian market through regional independent retailers, hospitality venues, and the company’s central brewery outlet.

title: Will California craft distillers face end of home deliveries?
summary:
Californians may suddenly have craft distillery deliveries halted at the end of the month, unless lawmakers intervene. db reports.

The post Will California craft distillers face end of home deliveries? appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Californians may suddenly have craft distillery deliveries halted at the end of the month, unless lawmakers intervene. db reports. Despite the fears, California’s wine industry, Teamsters union truck drivers and corporate alcohol wholesalers and distributors have rallied together to lobby the legislation. According to reports via CalMatters, Californians have been able to utilise the cocktail at home market by using alcohol delivered to their doorstep. Despite the trend, the sector is now in a predicament where it hopes it can block legislation and, following the pandemic-era rules that allowed craft distillers to ship spirits directly to their customers, make the rule permanent.

'I don't have a lot of hope'

During the Covid lockdowns, Governor Gavin Newsom issued an executive order that meant that craft distillers could send spirits directly to their customers’ homes in a bid to keep the industry alive and also raise morale for those stuck indoors and unable to get out to stores. However, in the years since, lawmakers passed what they called “temporary laws” which allowed the craft distillers — defined as those that produce up to 150,000 gallons a year — to continue to ship their spirits. Folsom Republican assembly member Josh Hoover said: “I don’t have a lot of hope that we’re going to be able to salvage this.” As Hoover highlighted, he has already tried to unsuccessfully amend one of these bills. He explained that the groups blocking his proposal have spent more than US$1 million lobbying the legislature and state government this year. Plus, they have donated at least 11 times that much to California politicians and their campaigns over the years.

Expenditure

The craft distillers, who have spent a fraction as much on state politics, say all that spending from the opposition, particularly from corporate spirits distributors, appears to have paid off. California Distillers Association acting editor director Cris Steller said: “They went directly to legislators’ offices and basically torpedoed any effort we came up with.” The fight has purportedly shown how decisions where wealthy and powerful interests can, according to Steller, “shape or kill policy in secret negotiations with lawmakers. Politicians, in turn, benefit when proposals die quietly because they don’t have to explain their decisions to voters”. Teamsters lobbyist Matt Broad said the group’s truck drivers aren’t opposed to allowing craft distillers to ship their product and just want them to use established shipping companies that have actual employees, including those that employ Teamsters, such as UPS. Broad told CalMatters: “We are absolutely not opposed to the little guys being able to ship directly to consumers, and in fact, we have a track record of supporting the proposal but with meaningful guardrails that protect our members and protect the public,” he told CalMatters. The California wine industry, which has been allowed to ship bottles directly to customers in California for many years, has also said that it isn’t opposed either. But its representative noted that wine sellers are cautious of giving craft alcohol sellers delivery rights when big spirits companies deserve the same. At present, wineries of any size can ship to their customers in California.

Less than a month to go

Although the US Postal Service prohibits most alcohol shipments to homes, California allows certain types of alcohol sellers to use private shipping companies. Although breweries are prohibited from shipping directly to California customers. Hoover said: “I’m always open to figuring this out, if there’s a way that we can make this work. … but I don’t have a lot of hope that this bill is going to preserve those provisions this year.” With less than a month left before the legislature finishes for the year on 31 August, Democratic leaders would likely need to sign off on changes. Wine & Spirits Wholesalers of America, the California Beer & Beverage Distributors and the California Family Beer Distributors wrote in a joint statement to CalMatters: “We oppose any effort to make DTC (direct to consumer) permanent,” the craft distilleries’ direct shipping “was always meant to be temporary pandemic relief, and it’s expiring exactly as designed, six years later” said the groups, which represent local and national companies that move many of America’s best-known beer, wine and spirits brands.

title: New Zealand’s Elephant Hill winery to be sold
summary:
The assets belonging to Elephant Hill in Hawke's Bay have been placed on the market with no guide price as the economics of New Zealand winemaking begin to unravel, according to one industry figure. db reports.

The post New Zealand’s Elephant Hill winery to be sold appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
The assets belonging to Elephant Hill in Hawke's Bay have been placed on the market with no guide price as the economics of New Zealand winemaking begin to unravel, according to one industry figure. db reports. A buyer is being sought for Elephant Hill in Hawke's Bay, including the estate's winery, cellar door, restaurant, vineyards, business assets, intellectual property, and wine inventory. The estate is available either as a going concern or may be sold off as individual assets, according to investment company Colliers, which is managing the sale. The property listing states that the sale provides "exceptional flexibility for purchasers seeking exposure to one or more segments of the wine, tourism, hospitality, or property sectors." No price guidance is being given for the assets, with interested parties encouraged to submit their best offers, suggesting that the owners may be looking to complete the sale quickly.

Unravelling economics

Speaking to the drinks business last month, Euan Mackay, MD for UK distributer Fells, said that the wine oversupply in New Zealand would make itself felt "from this vintage". In many ways, Mackay said, “the global market is moving faster than the wine world can cope with. It’s why there are lots of producers in Australia and New Zealand saying: ‘I’ve got a whole lot of wine that I don’t know what to do with,’ from plantings they made five to 10 years ago. The economics are beginning to unravel.” However, Hawke's Bay in New Zealand's North Island has experienced tiny, high-quality vintages in recent years. Many winemakers in the region saw their harvests shrink in 2023 following the devastation wrought by Cyclone Gabrielle. Phil Brodie, winemaker for Te Mata, told db that due to the cyclone, its total harvest for all grape varieties in 2023 was “about 50% of a usual year”. Hastings District Council mayor Sandra Hazlehurst revealed to db that "more than NZ$1.2 billion dollars worth of damage was done to our region" as a result of the storm, and that Hawke's Bay had "spent the last two years in full recovery.”

Flood damage

Much of the damage was caused by flooding, which deposited huge amounts of silt and debris on the region. “Masses of water came down… it was an all-out assault from the rivers,” said Hazlehurst. “All our trees and vineyards were neck-high in silt. Paddocks, fields and vineyards were absolutely decimated.” Clearing the silt alone cost Hastings around NZ$228 million. That being said, in 2025 wine volumes began to rebound, with Hawke’s Bay Winegrowers chairwoman Sally Duncan confirming that "over 32 million bottles" were expected to be made from that vintage. This year, Hawke's Bay experienced its earliest ever harvest start date, kicking off around 10 February, and according to Jancisrobinson.com "the consensus is that volumes will be less than average, particularly so in the shadow of the abundant 2025 harvest."

What might attract a buyer to Elephant Hill?

Located on the Te Awanga coastline in Hawke's Bay, Elephant Hill overlooks the Pacific Ocean towards Cape Kidnappers. Established in 2003 by Roger and Reydan Weiss, "few properties in New Zealand combine world-class wine, luxury hospitality, architectural distinction, and coastal beauty as seamlessly as Elephant Hill," claims Colliers. The estate's three diverse vineyards include 24 hectares planted at Te Awanga, 17.61ha at Gimblett Gravels, and 17.27ha at Bridge Pa, with Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Viognier on offer for white winemaking in addition to Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Syrah and Malbec for reds. All three vineyards are certified by Sustainable Winegrowers of New Zealand. Elephant Hill's wine offering is undoubtedly a premium one, with the producer's top wine, the red blend Hieronymous, retailing for up to NZ$200, depending on the vintage, while its Salomé Chardonnay is priced from around NZ$95.

A future beyond wine?

Hadley Brown, director of rural at Colliers Hawke’s Bay, said the Elephant Hill sale offers opportunities that extend well beyond wine. “What makes Elephant Hill particularly compelling is its ability to support a variety of future visions. For one purchaser, it may represent the continuation and expansion of an established premium winery. For another, it could become a luxury tourism destination that builds on the region's growing international profile,” Brown said. “Others may see the potential to further develop the hospitality offering, expand accommodation experiences, grow the events business, establish a high-end retreat, or create an agritourism enterprise that leverages the property's unique coastal location and existing brand recognition.” Mike Laven, rural & agribusiness special projects advisor at Colliers, added that the Elephant Hill brand could also be attractive to both domestic and international wine companies looking to add to their existing portfolio. “The Elephant Hill brand and associated wine business do not need to remain tied to the Te Awanga property," he said. "The intellectual property, wine inventory, and brand assets can continue to operate under separate ownership and from an alternative production facility, creating flexibility for purchasers seeking to acquire either the premium wine brand, the underlying property assets, or both.”

title: How wine PR has changed, according to an industry veteran
summary:
With a 50-year career in wine PR, Fiona Campbell has plenty to say about marketing drinks over the decades and tells Patrick Schmitt MW why the approach is different today.

The post How wine PR has changed, according to an industry veteran appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
With a 50-year career in wine PR, Fiona Campbell has plenty to say about marketing drinks over the decades, and tells Patrick Schmitt MW why the approach is different today.

Starring on our Desert Island Drinks podcast last month, Campbell revealed the eight special drinks of her lifetime, as well as the book and luxury she'd want to take with her if castaway, while also discussing some of the developments in wine PR – including giving some tips on the lasting rules of drinks marketing.

Initially, however, she drew some contrasts between the UK drinks trade she entered in the mid-70s and today's landscape.

"There's much more competition," she began. "London has always been seen as the international marketplace for wines, so everybody wants to get into the UK... but there are more retailers with different ways of selling wine."

Continuing, she said, "When I started, it was just the traditional wine merchants, and now you've got online marketing, and you've got the power of the supermarkets."

Social media

Of course, for much of her career, Campbell was dealing with little else but the printed word, and suggests that social media represents the biggest structural shift for anyone in wine PR.

She also warns those in drinks marketing that it's important to know which voices actually carry weight versus those that just claim to.

"I believe social media has to be controlled: there are certain commentators who know exactly what they're doing, and they have a great deal of influence. But there are also a number of others who set up as wine writers or wine commentators and don't have a following."

Press trips

Another marked change concerns a reduction in the amount of time journalists have to spend travelling.

"When I started doing Taylor's press trips, it was assumed that they'd [wine writers] have a full week to do a trip. Now that doesn't work out if you don't have many column inches in your paper to be paid for. So you've got to balance that too — I brought the trips down to two or three days."

The other shift concerns a move away from a concentrated set of print-based wine critics who had plenty of backing from their editors.

Looking back, she recalled, "They had the luxury of having full pages to write about what they wanted... they needed to have the visits to the vineyards to see how it's produced and find the stories there to make it interesting for their readers."

Such experts still exist, but today it's a more fragmented, influencer-driven community that wine PRs must engage with.

Quality and personality

Nevertheless, Campbell believes the basics of drinks marketing, particularly on a tight budget, haven't changed. Of any wine she promotes, she stressed: "First of all, it's got to be good, it's got to win the approval of the wine journalists."

Beyond that, she said, "You've got to give that wine a personality, and you can give that through meetings, tastings, and dinners with your client, with your winemakers, and then press trips to see where it's made, but you have to tailor those to the time that's available in a journalist's life."

This last point is perhaps key to those in drinks PR who may be frustrated when a blanket campaign falls to be picked up by the specialist – whatever form of media they work with.

As for Campbell's many other thoughts on working in the wine trade since the mid-70s, as well as her choice of drinks, please listen to the podcast by clicking here.

title: Ironhill India merges with US namesake in bankruptcy deal
summary:
Hyderabad-based Ironhill India, the country’s largest microbrewery chain, has rescued US company of the same name, Ironhill USA, from bankruptcy, creating a hospitality group with revenue of about ₹450 crore.

The post Ironhill India merges with US namesake in bankruptcy deal appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Hyderabad-based Ironhill India, the country’s largest microbrewery chain, has rescued US company of the same name, Ironhill USA, from bankruptcy, creating a hospitality group with revenue of about ₹450 crore. Ironhill India has invested about $7m (£5.5m) in the Pennsylvania-based craft beer business, including $4m earmarked to revive and reopen five outlets. The deal also sees Ironhill India acquire the US brewery, which was founded in 1996, out of bankruptcy. The combined group plans to expand to about 43 outlets by 2030, with 27 in India and 16 in the US. The integration gives Ironhill India access to the Ironhill global trademark, as well as established brewing expertise and operational systems in the US market.

“Joining forces with Ironhill US was a decision rooted in conviction in the brand’s legacy, the quality of its people, and the scale of what we can build together,” said Sree Harsha Vadlamudi, co-founder and board director of Ironhill India, according to Passionate in Marketing reports.

“India and the United States are two of the world’s most dynamic hospitality markets, and this partnership gives us a platform to operate across both with shared ambition and complementary strengths.”

Expansion plans

Ironhill India currently operates around 10 outlets. The group plans to grow its Indian network to 27 outlets while expanding its US presence to 16 locations. As part of the US revival, Ironhill has reopened locations in Center City Philadelphia, Hershey, Wilmington, Lancaster and Huntingdon Valley. The reopening has restored jobs for about 500 team members and vendors, according to the company. “Bringing Ironhill back has meant bringing 500 team members and vendors back to their jobs, their regulars, and to the craft they spent years perfecting,” Alexis Lundeen, director of operations at Ironhill USA told Passionate in Marketing. “The response from our communities across Philadelphia, Wilmington, Hershey, Lancaster, and Huntingdon Valley has been humbling.”

Envisioning a shared future

The two businesses will operate under shared brand, product and service standards. Their brewing and culinary teams will form a central innovation hub, developing new menus and brewing products drawing on expertise from both markets. Ironhill India was recognised with the Beer Asia Chairman’s Selection 2025, alongside several other industry awards. The group said it plans to pursue further expansion in international markets, with additional announcements expected during 2026 and 2027.

title: Helmsman Imports and Ankaa Global Logistics join forces
summary:
New York-based importer Helmsman Imports has teamed up with Ankaa Global Logistics, the third-party logistics arm of Southern Glazer’s, to provide warehousing and fulfilment services for its clients.

The post Helmsman Imports and Ankaa Global Logistics join forces appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
New York-based importer Helmsman Imports has teamed up with Ankaa Global Logistics, the third-party logistics arm of Southern Glazer’s, to provide warehousing and fulfilment services for its clients. Southern Glazer’s, the largest drinks distributor in the US, launched Ankaa in 2023 with the aim of establishing a premier logistic service provider for the drinks industry. Under the agreement, Helmsman Imports will gain access to Ankaa’s warehouse network, which currently include facilities in Shepherdsville, Kentucky, and Fairfield, California, to store and manage inventory for alcoholic brands in both the domestic and international market.  Ankaa brings extensive beverage alcohol supply chain experience to the partnership, including storage and value-added packaging capabilities. Its infrastructure is designed to address the regulatory and operational requirements involved in moving beverage alcohol through the supply chain after products clear customs. The partnership is also intended to address post-production logistics challenges faced by domestic brands expanding across multiple states or moving toward national distribution, particularly once finished products leave co-packers and require storage and fulfilment.

Delivering at scale

Through the arrangement, Helmsman clients will have access to managed warehouse storage, inventory visibility and outbound fulfilment services. The companies are also integrating their systems, allowing inventory data from Ankaa’s facilities to flow into Helmsman’s proprietary business intelligence platform, The Helm. “We built Helmsman because founders need an importer that understands their challenges at every step, not just the paperwork,” said Jeff Diego, founder and CEO of Helmsman Imports. “Fulfilment, storage, and how efficiently a distributor pickup happens are part of that same problem. Those pickups have to be seamless; that’s what actually gets a brand’s product to market on time.” Diego added that Helmman chose to partner with Ankaa as the company understands Helmsman Imports’ storage and fulfilment needs, and it has the facilities and expertise to deliver it at scale. Helmsman operates as a full-service importer of record, handling compliance filings, inventory management, accounts receivable and payable, chargeback processing and Certificate of Label Approval (COLA) submissions through its Helmsman App platform.

A natural fit

The Ankaa agreement adds physical warehouse capacity to that infrastructure, combining Helmsman’s compliance and financial services with Ankaa’s logistics and fulfilment capabilities for brands entering or expanding in the US market. “Our mission is to provide seamless vertical integration solutions for beverage alcohol suppliers that are efficient, transparent and differentiated,” added Drew Vermilion, senior vice president of supply chain at Southern Glazer’s Wine and Spirits. “Helmsman’s model as a full-service importer of record is a natural fit for what we’re building at Ankaa.” Southern Glazer’s operates in 47 markets with projected revenue of approximately US$25.5 billion. But weak demand is continuing to impact the US distribution market. Just last month, Southern Glazer’s announced 250 job cuts, alongside an expansion of its use of artificial intelligence, as rival RNDC began major restructuring following the loss of several high-profile supplier contracts including Brown-Forman, Treasury Wine Estates and Pernod Ricard. SGWS said that it is implementing a new way of doing business through a hybrid approach that will combine field sales, inside sales and digital commerce under the same roof. The consolidation, it says, will create a newly designed “Customer Solutions Team” to better serve an additional 1% of its clientele.

title: Tasting brings rare chance to discover Moldovan wine in the UK
summary:
With a long history, old vines and strong volume, Moldova seems poised to break through on the international wine scene. This September’s Moldova Uncorked tasting will give British drinks professionals and wine lovers a head start.

The post Tasting brings rare chance to discover Moldovan wine in the UK appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
With a long history, old vines and strong volume, Moldova seems poised to break through on the international wine scene. This September’s Moldova Uncorked tasting will give British drinks professionals and wine lovers a head start. Look at Moldova on paper, and you would see a country that, surely, should be on every wine lover’s lips. With 110,000 hectares under vine – often old vine plantings – it has more vineyards than South Africa. Its continental climate is uniformly warm, reliable but with diurnal variation to maintain freshness. Its grape varieties bridge trends: international varieties like Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay rub shoulders with the local Fetească family. In short, there is a host of reasons to pay attention to Moldovan wine. Its relative obscurity is an unfortunate circumstance of recent history; over the last 30 years, it has made an impressively rapid turn away from reliance on the Russian market and is now looking across Europe. Hence Moldova is making its case, including in the UK this year. On Saturday 12 September, Delapré Abbey in Northampton will become a playground for wine lovers with the arrival of Moldova Uncorked. 10 Moldovan wineries will come together to present more than 60 wines. Open to both consumers and the UK wine trade, it is set to confirm the growing buzz around the nation’s winemaking.

Building a presence

As a comprehensive day’s tasting, Modova Uncorked is a major opportunity for the UK wine trade – and indeed the country’s wine drinkers – to get to know Moldovan wine. As one of Europe’s fastest-growing producer nations, understanding Moldova makes inherent commercial sense. Yet the day is built around maximising opportunities rather than just showing off wines. Moldova Uncorked celebrates the learning opportunities and personal connections that power longstanding partnerships. Winemakers themselves will be on hand, explaining the expertise and craft that goes into each bottle. With many producers seeking UK representation, they will be able to make their case in person and establish direct contacts for future work. Moreover, the day’s masterclasses will mean that anyone not up to speed on Moldovan wine can quickly catch up. Experts will run through everything from climate and terroir to winemaking philosophy to indigenous grapes – the treasure trove that includes Viorica, Fetească Albă, Fetească Neagră and Rară Neagră. No prior knowledge is needed; Moldova Uncorked is for the aficionado and the newcomer alike.

Making Moldova accessible

Crucially, organisers Wine Chateau have designed the event to serve a broad swathe of the UK wine trade. Coming just after the summer holiday but before the Christmas rush, the tasting is at the perfect point in the calendar to explore new opportunities and expand the range of wines that you offer. Its venue, meanwhile, is both impressive and practical. The neoclassical mansion is 10 minutes from Northampton train station, which is just an hour from both London and Birmingham. Trade attendees can register for free tickets to the day’s event, while tickets for the general public cost £27.80 (at the early bird rate valid until the end of the month) or £109.05 for five tickets. All reservations can be made through Wine Chateau on this link.

title: Origin story: Armenian wine makes its comeback
summary:
With a heritage dating back thousands of years and a history tainted by Soviet rule, Armenia is now focused on resurrection, writes Anthony Rose.

The post Origin story: Armenian wine makes its comeback appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
With a heritage dating back thousands of years and a history tainted by Soviet rule, Armenia is now focused on resurrection, writes Anthony Rose. Back in May, the Concours Mondial de Bruxelles, a prestigious annual international wine competition famous for its rigorous blind tasting process, took place in Yerevan – a choice which was far from symbolic. In fact, the region pre-dates Rome. Armenia is a land of superlatives: it became the world’s first Christian nation in 301CE, is home to one of the oldest continuously written languages and, significantly, contains the site of the oldest winery yet discovered. Excavations of the Areni-1 cave in Vayots Dzor began in 2007, involving teams from the Universities of Oxford and California, and the site contains a complete winemaking installation dated to around 4,100BCE–4,000BCE, including wine press, fermentation vessels, storage jars, drinking cups and grape residues. Found alongside human remains, it was an ancient ritual site in which wine played an integral part. Nor is it an isolated find: the fortress of Teishebaini (Karmir Blur), unearthed near Yerevan in the 1940s and dating to the 8th century BCE, yielded seven cellars with 400 half-buried karases – Armenian clay vessels – with a capacity of 450,000 litres. Wine’s grip on Armenian civilisation runs deep. Which is why the tagline ‘Armenia, the oldest newest wine country’ is both irresistible and a little double-edged. The ancient heritage is archaeologically unimpeachable. The modern story of exile, dispossession, reinvention and the assertion of identity through wine, barely two decades old, is the more compelling one. Armenia is a small, landlocked nation bordered by Georgia, Azerbaijan, Turkey and Iran. At around 11,500 square miles, roughly the size of Belgium, it’s home to a population of three million people, though 7m–10m live outside its borders as part of the Armenian diaspora. The country sits on a high plateau to the east of Mount Ararat, a dormant volcano with a peak elevation of 5,137 metres, and the alleged resting place of Noah’s Ark. The Armenian language rises and falls in a lilting cadence; its elegantly curved script is unique. Yerevan, known as the Pink City for its 40 shades of volcanic pink stone, mingles ancient churches and neo-classical façades with Soviet brutalism. Tree-lined pavements are chock-full of cafés, the streets in constant logjam. Restaurants offer a varied cuisine focused on fresh vegetables and salads, herbs, grilled meats and herb-stuffed flatbreads. Above the arid valley floor, the twin snowcapped domes of Mount Ararat and its smaller sibling, Little Ararat, at 3,896m still higher than Mount Fuji, hover like floating clouds, seemingly following you wherever you go.

Wine country

Armenian wine country divides into five regions. Vayots Dzor is the established jewel: cool, high (950m–1,800m), with old vines and deep traditions surviving the Soviet era through remoteness; home to the Sev Areni and Voskehat grapes, and to producers such as Zorah, Hin-Areni and Yacoubian-Hobbs. Then there is Aragatsotn to the northwest, which sits on ancient volcanic soils from Mount Aragats and has seen the biggest recent investment, with Van Ardi, Voskevaz and ArmAs among its notable names. At nearly 6,000 hectares, Armavir is the largest region and the historic heart of brandy production, though MoonQ, Karas and Jraghatspanyan are among those recasting it as a serious wine zone. Ararat, the sunniest region and second largest, runs hot and low, producing full-bodied reds. Last but not least, Tavush, in the forested north-east, is the most rainfall-rich, historically important during the Soviet era, and home to producers Ijevan and Hovaz. The modern wine revival has three engines. The first is the Armenian diaspora, which brings money, international savoir-faire and passionate attachment to the homeland. The second is outside expertise: Alberto Antonini at Zorah, Paul Hobbs at Yacoubian-Hobbs and, until his untimely death, Michel Rolland at Karas. The third is institutional. The Vine and Wine Foundation of Armenia (VWFA) was established in 2016 with a mission to develop local viticulture, promote the competitiveness of Armenian wines internationally, create the Wine of Armenia brand, and increase both consumption and export volumes. It has organised international tastings, pursued GI development, campaigned to shift domestic consumption from vodka to wine, and lobbied successfully for the abolition of the winemaking licence fee. Armenian rhapsody: Queen guitarist Brian May features in the cellar at Voskevaz A subsidy programme introduced six years ago offers interest grace periods for new vineyard establishment, equipment subsidies, and 50% cost compensation for organic and sustainability certification. Its weakness, as MoonQ’s Tevan Poghosyan observes without rancour, is a minimum three-hectare land threshold that excludes the micro-producers making some of the most interesting wines; the smallest, most distinctive voices are precisely those least served.

Returners and refugees

The human stories that animate Armenian wine are, almost without exception, stories of leaving and coming back, or of being forced out and refusing to disappear. They take three distinct forms: the diaspora Armenian who returns by choice; the Artsakh Armenian displaced by war; and the international consultant drawn by curiosity and staying for conviction – and a fee. Zorik Gharibian represents the first category most vividly: a diaspora Armenian who grew up in Italy and built a successful career in fashion manufacturing. Arriving in Armenia as a tourist in 1998, he resolved to reconnect Armenian wine to its historical roots, establishing Zorah, a striking modern winery at 1,600m against a backdrop of reddish mountain peaks. “When Zorah began,” he recalls, “there was no interest in local varieties or traditional ageing methods. Such little interest as there was in wine was focused on international grape varieties and completely ignored the use of karas.” The stories of Artsakh, the disputed enclave seized by Azerbaijan in 2023, are harder. Andranik Manvelyan, Kataro’s winemaker, harvested grapes under shellfire in October 2020 within kilometres of active combat, escaped with 10,000 bottles of reserve Khndoghni, sold each for €100 to relaunch the winery, then delivered free wine to every customer in the following vintage. “We are Kataro because of them,” he says. In 2023, founder Grigory Avetissyan smuggled 1,200 Khndoghni cuttings back to Armenia in Russian peacekeepers’ trucks; they are growing at a new facility, a former Soviet silk building whose walls are being painted with murals replicating those of the original winery. Kataro is the only one of Artsakh’s 15 former wineries to have restarted production. The new vines won’t be ready until 2031-32. “It’s not about the wine,” says Manvelyan. “It’s about the emotions that will be in the bottle.” Tevan Poghosyan’s story runs parallel. A diplomat and former MP born in Stepanakert, he started making wine in 2004 – just 100 bottles a year. After the 2020 war, his children pressed him to turn professional. MoonQ, from the Artsakh dialect word for ‘we’, was born, devoted to Nrneni, a variety until recently considered lost, of which only half a hectare survives. A cross of Cabernet Sauvignon, Alicante Bouschet and Saperavi, it is unique in Armenian viticulture. Going to pot: making karases is a lost art

Karas, Kakhani and the scientific method

Winemaking techniques are as varied as the producers themselves, but one vessel appears everywhere: the karas, Armenia’s large, egg-shaped clay amphora, coated with beeswax, with a narrow mouth. It differs from the Georgian qvevri, which is buried entirely underground and round-bottomed, in being lighter in colour, made from limestone-rich clay, and traditionally stored in elevated rows or terraces, rather than buried. It is both a symbol and a technical tool. Gharibian has spent years systematising the karas, settling on the “two-thirds buried, one-third exposed” approach documented at Karmir Blur 3,000 years ago: the buried section provides temperature stability; the exposed section permits gentle micro-oxygenation. “Clay is a fundamentally neutral material,” he says. “The karas doesn’t give or take anything from wine; it allows it to express the potential of the fruit and terroir.” The practical problem is existential: Soviet rule interrupted the tradition of karas-making, and there is today nobody in Armenia who knows how to make them properly. The supply, sourced from old rural families, abandoned farmyards and archaeological salvage, is finite and dwindling. The karas has become the marketing emblem of Armenian wine’s ancient credentials at precisely the moment when authentic vessels are running out.

Volcanic terrain

Voskevaz, a family-owned estate founded in 1932 that sits on entirely volcanic terrain in Aragatsotn, pairs karas with the Kakhani method: the drying of whole grape bunches on wires, concentrating flavours à la Amarone, as village winemakers have done for centuries. Architecturally, Voskevaz is a hoot: a mock-medieval Disneyland-meets-Game of Thrones series of fortresses and towers whose hilarious kitschness belies the fact that this is a serious winemaking operation, making whites and reds from indigenous varieties of the highest quality. You arrive with a smirk and leave with a broad smile. Gevorkian, based in a former Soviet glass production facility in Yerevan, studied early sources, codified the bunch-drying method, registered it with the government and relaunched it in 2012. Three expressions cover the range: Kes-Kakhani (50% fresh, 50% dried; 14% ABV), Classic Kakhani (100% dried; the Amarone equivalent at 16%); and Sweet Kakhani (dried to 40° Brix; 100g/l–120g/l residual sugar). The winery also makes pét-nat, orange wine and fruit wines including pomegranate wine, its most important product commercially. Artem Jraghatspanyan takes an entirely different path: rigorous, scientific, data-driven. His family made wine in Bambakashat, Armavir from the 1890s, but Jraghatspanyan spent 21 years at the Yerevan Brandy Company, conducting 200 trials over eight years before registering the winery in 2018. He works with 10 grape varieties, vinifying six, and buys grapes at 10%-12% above market price across 15 contracted hectares, all within a few kilometres of the winery. Bible story: Mount Ararat is said to be the last resting place of Noah’s ark

The Soviet legacy

The Soviet period haunts Armenian wine at every turn, in the infrastructure inherited, the traditions suppressed and the identities forcibly redirected. The Yerevan Brandy Company is a reminder that Armenia’s viticultural identity was for most of the past century distilled rather than bottled. The Soviet authorities designated Georgia as wine producer and Armenia as brandy supplier. Winston Churchill was a devotee of Ararat brandy, and it remains as good as any Cognac or Armagnac today, but the designation came at a cost: the neglect of indigenous grape varieties and the near-extinction of the karasmaking craft. The Ijevan Wine and Brandy Factory in Tavush, founded in 1951, carries this history in its walls: eight underground rooms from the 1930s, four metres below ground with paraffin wax-coated walls, served as a clandestine winemaking facility when production had been officially redirected to Georgia and Moldova. Today Ijevan produces around 2m bottles annually from seven indigenous varieties, with an excellent premium range made by hand with natural fermentation; no added yeasts, no bentonite. One further consequence of Soviet-era isolation: limited access to French oak barrels, which pushed producers towards indigenous Caucasian or Armenian oak instead. The barrels are crafted with bespoke toasting profiles to suit the wood’s tight grain, and over multiple vintages the hand-assembled staves naturally shift, giving them a slightly uneven appearance. “As long as it doesn’t leak, it is fine,” one winemaker says, with typical Armenian directness. The irony is sharp: Artsakh’s oak forests, which supplied much of the wood, are now inaccessible following the 2023 Azerbaijani takeover.

New directions

Against this backdrop of ancient traditions and Soviet shadows, newer producers are finding their own paths. Hin-Areni, founded in 2013 in the village of Areni itself, farms 25ha of certified organic vines on their own roots at an altitude of 1,250m and produces clean, precise wines that serve as a good introduction to the two varieties that dominate Armenian wine production, Voskehat and Sev Areni. Hovaz Wine Rooms in Dilijan, opened in 2022 by a women-led team, contracts with local farmers, pays above-market prices and controls all vineyard processes. Its name is the Armenian word for leopard, marking the species’ return to Armenia. Its signature experience invites visitors to participate in the disgorgement of a traditional-method wine and leave with a personalised, numbered bottle from a limited edition of 1,500. Dominating presence: Mount Ararat and Little Ararat loom over Armenia’s capital, Yerevan On Yerevan’s Saryan Street, known locally as ‘Wine Street’, In Vino and a cluster of neighbouring bars (Urban, DV Wine Library, Decant, Collective, Vino&Vino) reflect an increasingly confident domestic wine culture. Mariam Saghatelyan, an Armenian-American sommelier who co-founded In Vino in 2012, recalls there being “maybe 10 drinkable Armenian wines” when she started. Today the bar stocks over 600 local labels and has become both a showcase for the renaissance and a community hub, with a growing emphasis on lower-alcohol wines and pét-nat. Zaruhi Muradyan, executive director of the VWFA, described hosting Concours Mondial de Bruxelles in Armenia as “not only an honour, but a strategic opportunity to present Armenia’s wine heritage, contemporary winemaking and growing international ambitions to some of the most influential voices in the global wine world.” Armenia’s Minister of Economy Gevorg Papoyan highlighted wine as an increasingly important export category, with the country actively seeking stronger trade relationships in European markets. Armenia’s wine renaissance is not primarily a lifestyle story. It is a story about a people using wine, as they have for 6,000 years, to say: we are still here and we’re going places.

Armenian wine: facts and figures

• Production peaked at 14.1 million litres in 2023 before falling sharply to 10m litres in 2024 and 7.7m litres in 2025, the lowest since 2016. • 178 active winemaking companies and approximately 12,000 growers. • 95 producers make fewer than 5,000 bottles (up from only 11 in 2020); only five companies exceed 1m bottles. • Total cultivated vineyard area: around 13,000 hectares (roughly 10% table grapes, 15%–20% wine grapes, the rest used for brandy). • Total grape wine exports in 2025: approximately 4m litres, worth US$19m, down from the 2022 peak of 4.8m litres, although value has held up better, suggesting a shift towards more expensive wines. • Fruit wine exports add a further 4.4m litres (US$12.3m), making Armenia’s total export picture more complex than grape wine alone suggests. • Russia’s dominance is stark and persistent: 80.2% of exports by volume in 2025 (83.2% in 2023). In absolute terms, 3.24m litres worth US$13.6m. • Other leading markets: US (4.9% export share), France (2.3%), Poland (1.6%), Belgium (1.3%). All markets outside Russia combined account for less than 20% of volume. • The UK imported nearly 20,000 litres worth US$124,000 in 2025, up sharply from US$52,749 in 2024. • Per capita wine consumption has risen from 2.0 litres in 2016 to 4.8 litres in 2025, a 140% increase in nine years, driven by the government’s pro-wine campaign. Anthony Rose visited Armenia as a judge at the Concours Mondial de Bruxelles and as a guest of the VWFA. For tasting notes and scores of Anthony’s favourite 25 wines, please see his Substack column.

title: United Spirits accused of ‘misleading’ whisky maturation claims
summary:
A week after India's food safety regulator banned the sale of certain spirits because of using improper flavourings, it has extended its labelling wrangle with Diageo subsidiary United Spirits. Ron Emler reports.

The post United Spirits accused of ‘misleading’ whisky maturation claims appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
A week after India's food safety regulator banned the sale of certain spirits because of using improper flavourings, it has extended its labelling wrangle with Diageo subsidiary United Spirits. Ron Emler reports. According to Reuters, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has accused Diageo subsidiary United Spirits Limited (USL) of misleadingly claiming that a best-selling ​whisky is “matured in American oak casks". The FSSAI alleged that the label says it is "matured in American oak casks", but that "your product has a grain neutral spirit as second ingredient ‌after demineralised ⁠water, and major portion is non-matured spirit." "The complete alcohol is not matured in wood cask as claimed on the label, and therefore misleading the consumer," it said. "Any claim regarding age of the spirit used in the product must refer to the youngest spirit used in the mix, not the oldest."

Best seller

Royal ​Challenge is one of Diageo's top-selling products in India, selling more than 4.5 million nine-litre cases. Its front label says: "A rich blend ⁠of Indian ​grain spirit & imported Scotches, matured in American oak casks". Its back label ​says it contains "demineralised water, grain neutral spirit, Scotch. Contains permitted natural colour ... and added nature identical (whisky) flavouring substances". Reuters also reports that the FSSAI notice said that Diageo's mention of "Scotch" is vague ​and "does not inform its true characteristics", and that the company must say what "Scotch" is used.

Artificial flavouring

The FSSAI announced last week it had ​prohibited sales of Diageo's Royal Challenge Whisky made in Madhya Pradesh and some whisky and ​rum brands made in other Indian states by Diageo and India's Inbrew for using artificial flavouring, ⁠such as whisky and rum flavours, rather than proper ageing and ingredients. The industry says it complies with the law. USL told Reuters that it remains committed to the highest quality standards and was "actively engaging with FSSAI to address their queries on labelling". The company has told stock exchanges that it anticipates no financial implications from the ​ban but that it is monitoring developments closely.

Increasing scrutiny

The crackdown on India's US$40 billion alcohol industry is part of increasing official scrutiny of labelling by liquor companies, energy drink ​makers such as PepsiCo and food producers over what it believes is incorrect labelling and weak compliance. The whisky ban ⁠covers Diageo's Antiquity Blue Whisky and Royal Challenge, made in Madhya Pradesh, as well as Inbrew's Bagpiper Deluxe Whisky and Old Cask Deluxe XXX Rum, also produced in that same state.
